rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The heavens are vast, elevated and adorned with moving and fixed stars and revolving spheres; earth is dense, low, and filled with varied terrain, settlement, and benefits.
rows.anchor: ارتفاعها واتساعها وكواكبها السيارة والثوابت ودوران فلكها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Night and day succeed one another without delay; their lengths vary and each can gain time from the other.
rows.anchor: وتارة يطول هذا ويقصر هذا، وتارة يأخذ هذا من هذا ثم يتقارضان

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ships cross the sea by God's subjection of it, carrying people's livelihoods and goods between regions.
rows.anchor: في تسخير البحر لحمل السفن من جانب إلى جانب لمعاش الناس

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Rain revives dead earth, as another passage illustrates through crops, gardens, springs, and fruits.
rows.anchor: آية لهم الأرض الميتة أحييناها وأخرجنا منها حبا فمنه يأكلون

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God spreads creatures of differing forms, colors, uses, and sizes, knows them all, and provides for them.
rows.anchor: على اختلاف أشكالها وألوانها ومنافعها وصغرها وكبرها، وهو يعلم ذلك كله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Winds alternate between mercy and punishment, herald clouds, drive, gather, scatter, and redirect them.
rows.anchor: تارة تأتي بالرحمة وتارة تأتي بالعذاب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Wind names and directions are related to how they pass the Kaaba: southern, Yemen-facing, eastern ṣabā, and western dabūr.
rows.anchor: تأتي من الجنوب وهي الشامية، وتارة تأتي من ناحية اليمن وتارة صبا، وهي الشرقية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Many books discuss the languages and rules of winds, rain, and stellar weather signs, but their detailed treatment is lengthy here.
rows.anchor: وقد صنف الناس في الرياح والمطر والأنواء كتبا كثيرة فيما يتعلق بلغاتها وأحكامها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Clouds travel between heaven and earth under God's control, directed to whichever lands and places He wills.
rows.anchor: أي: سائر بين السماء والأرض

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: These phenomena plainly demonstrate God's oneness and invite rational reflection, as the passage about thoughtful remembrance also says.
rows.anchor: في هذه الأشياء دلالات بينة على وحدانية الله تعالى

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Quraysh asked Muhammad to make al-Ṣafā gold so they could buy horses and weapons, believe, and fight with him; after their pledge, he declined the threatened punishment and asked time to invite them gradually.
rows.anchor: عن ابن عباس قال: أتت قريش محمدا صلى الله عليه وسلم فقالوا: يا محمد إنما نريد أن تدعو ربك

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: A second transmission adds the challenge that Quraysh could already see signs greater than turning al-Ṣafā to gold.
rows.anchor: وزاد في آخره: وكيف يسألونك عن الصفا وهم يرون من الآيات ما هو أعظم من الصفا

rows.speaker: عطاء
rows.claim: After 2:163 was revealed in Medina, Quraysh in Mecca asked how one God could suffice for everyone; this verse's signs taught them that He is the one Lord and creator of all.
rows.anchor: قال: نزلت على النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم بالمدينة: {وإلهكم إله واحد

rows.speaker: أبو الضحى
rows.claim: When the polytheists demanded a sign after hearing that God is one, this verse's signs were revealed in response.
rows.anchor: عن أبي الضحى قال: لما نزلت: {وإلهكم إله واحد} إلى آخر الآية، قال المشركون:

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The signs in creation teach that God is one, the deity of everything and creator of everything.
rows.anchor: فبهذا يعلمون أنه إله واحد، وأنه إله كل شيء وخالق كل شيء

none: The segment only gives another chain transmitting Abu al-Duha's preceding report, without adding its content.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A report describes the earlier rule: people could eat, drink, and have sex until sleep; an Anṣārī named Ṣirma worked while fasting, slept without food after ʿIshāʾ, and woke fasting and exhausted; ʿUmar had intercourse after sleeping, and the verse then came down.
rows.anchor: وكانوا يأكلون ويشربون ويأتون النساء ما لم يناموا، فإذا ناموا امتنعوا، ثم إن رجلا من الأنصار

rows.speaker: عائشة
rows.claim: ʿĀʾisha reports that ʿĀshūrāʾ had been fasted, then after Ramadan fasting became obligatory, people could choose to fast it or break the fast; Ibn ʿUmar and Ibn Masʿūd report the same.
rows.anchor: أنها قالت: كان عاشوراء يصام، فلما نزل فرض رمضان كان من شاء صام ومن شاء أفطر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: This verse relaxes the early rule, under which eating, drinking, and intercourse after breaking the fast stopped at ʿIshāʾ or sleep, whichever came first, a source of hardship.
rows.anchor: هذه رخصة من الله تعالى للمسلمين، ورفع لما كان عليه الأمر في ابتداء الإسلام، فإنه

rows.speaker: ابن عباس، عطاء، مجاهد، سعيد بن جبير، طاوس، سالم بن عبد الله، عمرو بن دينار، الحسن، قتادة
rows.claim: These authorities explain al-rafath here as sexual intercourse.
rows.anchor: ابن عباس، وعطاء، ومجاهد، وسعيد بن جبير، وطاوس، وسالم بن عبد الله، وعمرو بن دينار

rows.speaker: الزهري، الضحاك، إبراهيم النخعي، السدي، عطاء الخراساني، مقاتل بن حيان
rows.claim: These authorities likewise interpret al-rafath as intercourse.
rows.anchor: والحسن، وقتادة، والزهري، والضحاك، وإبراهيم النخعي، والسدي، وعطاء الخراساني، ومقاتل بن حيان

rows.speaker: ابن عباس، مجاهد، سعيد بن جبير، الحسن، قتادة، السدي، مقاتل بن حيان
rows.claim: They explain spouses being garments for one another as each being a source of comfort and repose for the other.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس، ومجاهد، وسعيد بن جبير، والحسن، وقتادة، والسدي، ومقاتل بن حيان: يعني هن سكن لكم

rows.speaker: الربيع بن أنس
rows.claim: Al-Rabīʿ gives a related metaphor: each spouse is the other's covering or blanket.
rows.anchor: وقال الربيع بن أنس: هن لحاف لكم وأنتم لحاف لهن

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Because spouses mingle, touch, and lie together, allowing intercourse on Ramadan nights removes hardship and embarrassment.
rows.anchor: أن الرجل والمرأة كل منهما يخالط الآخر ويماسه ويضاجعه، فناسب أن يرخص لهم

rows.speaker: شاعر غير مسمى
rows.claim: An anonymous poetic line depicts the woman as her partner's garment when he embraces her, illustrating the metaphor.
rows.anchor: إذا ما الضجيع ثنى جيدها … تداعت فكانت عليه لباسا

rows.speaker: البراء بن عازب
rows.claim: Al-Barāʾ recounts that Qays ibn Ṣirma worked in his field while fasting, fell asleep before eating, and collapsed the next day; after the Prophet was told, the verse was revealed and people rejoiced.
rows.anchor: كان أصحاب النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم إذا كان الرجل صائما فنام قبل أن يفطر، لم يأكل إلى مثلها

rows.speaker: البراء بن عازب
rows.claim: Al-Barāʾ says that during Ramadan people initially avoided women all month and some wronged themselves, prompting the phrase that God knew they had been betraying themselves and then pardoned them.
rows.anchor: لما نزل صوم رمضان كانوا لا يقربون النساء، رمضان كله، وكان رجال يخونون أنفسهم، فأنزل الله:

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās says that after ʿIshāʾ Muslims initially abstained from food and women until the next night; after some, including ʿUmar, broke the rule, they complained and the verse permitted intimacy.
rows.anchor: النساء والطعام إلى مثلها من القابلة، ثم إن أناسا من المسلمين أصابوا من النساء والطعام

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: In another report, before the fasting rule was changed people ate and had sex until sleep; ʿUmar had intercourse after sleeping, confessed to the Prophet, and the verse was revealed.
rows.anchor: إن الناس كانوا قبل أن ينزل في الصوم ما نزل فيهم يأكلون ويشربون، ويحل لهم شأن النساء، فإذا نام أحدهم

rows.speaker: أبو هريرة
rows.claim: Abū Hurayra's report says ʿUmar had intercourse after ʿIshāʾ, while Ṣirma slept after sunset without a full meal and later ate after waking; the incident occasioned the verse.
rows.anchor: وإن عمر بن الخطاب أصاب أهله بعد صلاة العشاء، وأن صرمة بن قيس الأنصاري غلبته عينه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In these reports, al-rafath means intercourse, and spouses are described as each other's covering while they had eaten, drunk, and had sex after ʿIshāʾ.
rows.anchor: أحل لكم ليلة الصيام الرفث إلى نسائكم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abū Hurayra’s account concludes that the verse was revealed in response to companions’ infractions of the former night-time fasting restrictions.
rows.anchor: فأنزل الله عند ذلك: {أحل لكم ليلة الصيام الرفث إلى نسائكم}

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Eating and drinking remain lawful until dawn becomes distinct, after which the fast is completed until night; this is God's pardon and mercy.
rows.anchor: وكلوا واشربوا حتى يتبين لكم الخيط الأبيض من الخيط الأسود من الفجر

rows.speaker: عمر بن الخطاب
rows.claim: ʿUmar said that when he sought his wife after she had gone to sleep, she said she was asleep; he assumed she was making an excuse, had intercourse, and the verse was revealed concerning him.
rows.anchor: قال: قام عمر بن الخطاب، رضي الله عنه، فقال: يا رسول الله، إني أردت أهلي البارحة

rows.speaker: عبد الله بن كعب بن مالك
rows.claim: A report from Kaʿb ibn Mālik describes ʿUmar and Kaʿb having intercourse after sleep under the former rule; ʿUmar told the Prophet, and the verse followed. Mujāhid, ʿAṭāʾ, ʿIkrima, al-Suddī, and Qatāda also link it to ʿUmar, others like him, and Ṣirma.
rows.anchor: فوجد امرأته قد نامت، فأرادها، فقالت: إني قد نمت! فقال: ما نمت! ثم وقع بها. وصنع كعب بن مالك مثل ذلك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The ruling then allowed intercourse, food, and drink throughout the night as mercy, concession, and kindness.
rows.anchor: فأباح الجماع والطعام والشراب في جميع الليل رحمة ورخصة ورفقا

rows.speaker: أبو هريرة، ابن عباس، أنس، شريح القاضي، مجاهد، عكرمة، سعيد بن جبير، عطاء، الربيع بن أنس، السدي، زيد بن أسلم، الحكم بن عتبة، مقاتل بن حيان، الحسن البصري، الضحاك، قتادة
rows.claim: These authorities interpret seeking what God has ordained as seeking offspring.
rows.anchor: قال أبو هريرة، وابن عباس (4) وأنس، وشريح القاضي، ومجاهد، وعكرمة، وسعيد بن جبير، وعطاء

rows.speaker: عبد الرحمن بن زيد بن أسلم
rows.claim: Ibn Zayd instead interprets the phrase as referring to intercourse.
rows.anchor: وقال عبد الرحمن بن زيد بن أسلم: {وابتغوا ما كتب الله لكم} يعني: الجماع

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī reports from Ibn ʿAbbās that the phrase refers to Laylat al-Qadr.
rows.anchor: عن ابن عباس: {وابتغوا ما كتب الله لكم} قال: ليلة القدر

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: Qatāda offers two broad readings: seek the concession God prescribed, or what God made lawful.
rows.anchor: قال قتادة: وابتغوا الرخصة التي كتب الله لكم. وقال سعيد عن قتادة

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Asked whether to read wa-ibtaghū or wa-ittabiʿū, Ibn ʿAbbās allowed either but favored the first reading.
rows.anchor: قال: أيتهما شئت: عليك بالقراءة الأولى

rows.speaker: ابن جرير
rows.claim: Ibn Jarīr prefers the verse's wording to be understood broadly, encompassing all the reported interpretations.
rows.anchor: واختار ابن جرير أن الآية أعم من هذا كله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Food, drink, and intercourse are permitted throughout the night until dawn; the white thread is daylight and the black thread is night, with “from dawn” removing ambiguity.
rows.anchor: وعبر عن ذلك بالخيط الأبيض من الخيط الأسود، ورفع اللبس بقوله: {من الفجر}

rows.speaker: سهل بن سعد
rows.claim: Sahl reports that some tied white and black strings to their legs and ate until they could distinguish them; the added words “from dawn” clarified that night and day were intended.
rows.anchor: وكان رجال إذا أرادوا الصوم، ربط أحدهم في رجليه الخيط الأبيض والخيط الأسود، فلا يزال يأكل

rows.speaker: عدي بن حاتم
rows.claim: ʿAdī placed a black and a white cord under his pillow and could not distinguish them; the Prophet explained that the image meant night darkness and day whiteness, not literal cords.
rows.anchor: عمدت إلى عقالين، أحدهما أسود والآخر أبيض، قال: فجعلتهما تحت وسادتي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Prophet's remark that ʿAdī's pillow was broad refers to the cords spanning a width as broad as the east and west; another Bukhārī wording makes the explanation explicit.
rows.anchor: بياض النهار وسواد الليل. فيقتضي أن يكون بعرض المشرق والمغرب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Some took “your nape is broad” to mean dullness, but Ibn Kathīr calls that weak; it instead relates to the broad pillow and nape.
rows.anchor: ففسره بعضهم بالبلادة، وهو ضعيف. بل يرجع إلى هذا؛ لأنه إذا كان وساده عريضا

rows.speaker: عدي بن حاتم
rows.claim: Asked whether the white and black threads were actual cords, the Prophet told ʿAdī that the intended contrast was night darkness and daylight.
rows.anchor: قلت: يا رسول الله، ما الخيط الأبيض من الخيط الأسود، أهما الخيطان؟ قال: "إنك لعريض القفا إن أبصرت الخيطين"

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Because the verse permits eating until dawn, taking the lawful concession makes the pre-dawn meal recommended; accepting concessions is beloved.
rows.anchor: وفي إباحته تعالى جواز الأكل إلى طلوع الفجر، دليل على استحباب السحور

rows.speaker: أنس
rows.claim: The Prophet urged people to eat suḥūr, saying that it contains blessing.
rows.anchor: عن أنس قال: قال رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم: "تسحروا فإن في السحور بركة"

rows.speaker: عمرو بن العاص
rows.claim: The Prophet said the pre-dawn meal distinguishes the Muslim fast from the fast of the People of the Book.
rows.anchor: عن عمرو بن العاص رضي الله عنه، قال: قال رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم: "إن فصل

rows.speaker: أبو سعيد
rows.claim: A report says suḥūr is blessed and should not be neglected, even if one only takes a sip of water; God and His angels bless those who eat it.
rows.anchor: قال رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم: "السحور أكلة بركة؛ فلا تدعوه، ولو أن أحدكم يجرع جرعة من ماء، فإن الله وملائكته يصلون

rows.speaker: أنس، زيد بن ثابت
rows.claim: Anas and Zayd say they ate suḥūr with the Prophet, then went to prayer; the interval was about the time needed to recite fifty verses, showing it was delayed toward dawn.
rows.anchor: تسحرنا مع رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم، ثم قمنا إلى الصلاة. قال أنس: قلت لزيد: كم كان بين الأذان والسحور؟ قال

rows.speaker: أبو ذر
rows.claim: The Prophet said the community would remain in good condition while people hastened to break the fast and delayed suḥūr.
rows.anchor: لا تزال أمتي بخير ما عجلوا الإفطار وأخروا السحور

rows.speaker: حذيفة بن اليمان
rows.claim: Ḥudhayfa reports eating suḥūr with the Prophet when it seemed to be day though the sun had not risen; because ʿĀṣim alone transmitted it, Ibn Kathīr reads it as near dawn and cites 65:2's use of reaching a term for approaching it. Many early authorities allowed suḥūr close to dawn.
rows.anchor: تسحرنا مع رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم، وكان النهار إلا أن الشمس لم تطلع

rows.speaker: بعضهم، ابن جرير
rows.claim: Ibn Jarīr reports an opinion that abstention begins only at sunrise; Ibn Kathīr rejects it as contrary to the verse's explicit dawn cutoff and says no scholar can firmly hold it.
rows.anchor: أنه إنما يجب الإمساك من طلوع الشمس كما يجوز الإفطار بغروبها. قلت: وهذا القول ما أظن أحدا من أهل العلم

rows.speaker: عائشة
rows.claim: The Prophet said not to let Bilāl's night call prevent suḥūr; eat until Ibn Umm Maktūm calls, since he waits until dawn.
rows.anchor: أذان بلال عن سحوركم، فإنه ينادي بليل، فكلوا واشربوا حتى تسمعوا أذان ابن أم مكتوم

rows.speaker: طلق بن علي
rows.claim: The Prophet described the true dawn as a horizontal red light across the horizon, not a vertical brightness rising upward.
rows.anchor: ليس الفجر المستطيل في الأفق ولكنه المعترض الأحمر

rows.speaker: سمرة بن جندب
rows.claim: Samura reports that neither Bilāl's call nor the vertically elongated dawn ends suḥūr; the relevant dawn spreads across the horizon.
rows.anchor: لا يمنعكم من سحوركم أذان بلال ولا الفجر المستطيل، ولكن الفجر المستطير في الأفق

rows.speaker: محمد بن عبد الرحمن بن ثوبان
rows.claim: A good mursal report distinguishes a harmless vertical dawn like a wolf's tail from the horizontal dawn that permits prayer and forbids food.
rows.anchor: الفجر فجران، فالذي كأنه ذنب السرحان لا يحرم شيئا، وأما المستطير الذي يأخذ الأفق

rows.speaker: ابن عباس، عطاء
rows.claim: They distinguish two dawns: a vertical glow does not prohibit drink, begin prayer, or make pilgrimage time expire; only light spreading across mountain tops does so. Ibn Kathīr calls their chain sound and says other early authorities reported likewise.
rows.anchor: سمعت ابن عباس يقول: هما فجران، فأما الذي يسطع في السماء فليس يحل ولا يحرم شيئا

rows.speaker: جمهور العلماء، الأئمة الأربعة
rows.claim: Because dawn ends the permission for intercourse, food, and drink, someone who wakes in a state of major ritual impurity may wash and complete the fast; the four imams and majority rely on reports that the Prophet did so.
rows.anchor: وهذا مذهب الأئمة الأربعة وجمهور العلماء سلفا وخلفا، لما رواه البخاري ومسلم

rows.speaker: أبو هريرة
rows.claim: A report says that if dawn prayer is called while someone is sexually impure, he should not fast; Ibn Kathīr notes its good chain and transmissions in the two Ṣaḥīḥs and elsewhere.
rows.anchor: عن أبي هريرة، عن رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم أنه قال: "إذا نودي للصلاة -صلاة الصبح -وأحدكم جنب فلا يصم يومئذ"

rows.speaker: ابن حزم
rows.claim: Ibn Ḥazm says the report forbidding a fast after waking sexually impure was abrogated by this verse; Ibn Kathīr calls that remote because chronology is absent and apparently points the other way.
rows.anchor: وادعى ابن حزم أنه منسوخ بهذه الآية الكريمة، وهو بعيد أيضا، وأبعد؛ إذ لا تاريخ

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The closest and most comprehensive reconciliation reads “he has no fast” as denying its perfection, not its validity, preserving the permission established by ʿĀʾisha's and Umm Salama's reports.
rows.anchor: ومنهم من حمل حديث أبي هريرة على نفي الكمال "فلا صوم له" لحديث عائشة وأم سلمة الدالين على الجواز. وهذا المسلك أقرب الأقوال

rows.speaker: عمر بن الخطاب
rows.claim: The Prophet explained that a fast is considered ended when night advances from one side and day withdraws from the other, establishing sunset as the breaking point.
rows.anchor: عن أمير المؤمنين عمر بن الخطاب، رضي الله عنه، قال: قال رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم: "إذا أقبل الليل من هاهنا وأدبر النهار من هاهنا، فقد أفطر الصائم"

rows.speaker: سهل بن سعد الساعدي
rows.claim: The Prophet said people remain in good condition so long as they hasten to break the fast.
rows.anchor: لا يزال الناس بخير ما عجلوا الفطر

rows.speaker: أبو هريرة
rows.claim: A divine report says God's most beloved servants are those who hasten to break their fast; al-Tirmidhī grades this report ḥasan gharīb.
rows.anchor: عن أبي هريرة، عن النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم: "يقول الله، عز وجل: إن أحب عبادي إلي أعجلهم فطرا"

rows.speaker: ليلى امرأة بشير بن الخصاصية
rows.claim: When Laylā wanted to fast two days continuously, Bishr cited the Prophet's ban on continuous fasting and his instruction to finish at night and then break the fast; an Ibn ʿAsākir report adds that the Prophet's own continuous fast was a special exception and cites this verse.
rows.anchor: يفعل ذلك النصارى، ولكن صوموا كما أمركم الله، وأتموا الصيام إلى الليل، فإذا كان الليل فأفطروا

rows.speaker: أبو هريرة
rows.claim: The Prophet forbade joining one day's fast to the next without a break; when companions continued, he fasted with them for two days and nights, then said he could have extended it longer. The report is in both Ṣaḥīḥ collections.
rows.anchor: قال رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم: "لا تواصلوا". قالوا: يا رسول الله، إنك تواصل. قال: "فإني لست مثلكم، إني أبيت يطعمني ربي ويسقيني"

rows.speaker: عائشة
rows.claim: ʿĀʾisha says the Prophet forbade continuous fasting out of mercy for his followers, explaining that God fed and gave him drink.
rows.anchor: نهى رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم عن الوصال، رحمة لهم، فقالوا: إنك تواصل.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Continuous fasting was a special prophetic capacity; Ibn Kathīr says the apparent feeding and drinking were spiritual rather than physical, citing a poem about memory distracting a lover from food and drink.
rows.anchor: والأظهر أن ذلك الطعام والشراب في حقه إنما كان معنويا لا حسيا، وإلا فلا يكون مواصلا مع الحسي

rows.speaker: أبو سعيد الخدري
rows.claim: The Prophet allowed anyone wishing to continue fasting to extend only until suḥūr, while explaining his own special capacity; another report invites a fasting woman to follow the Prophet's family's suḥūr-to-suḥūr practice.
rows.anchor: فأيكم أراد أن يواصل فليواصل إلى السحر

rows.speaker: علي
rows.claim: ʿAlī reports that the Prophet would continue fasting from one suḥūr to the next.
rows.anchor: أن النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم كان يواصل من السحر إلى السحر

rows.speaker: عبد الله بن الزبير، سلف آخرون
rows.claim: Ibn al-Zubayr and other early Muslims continued for several days; Ibn Kathīr says they likely did so as self-discipline or understood the prohibition as compassionate guidance, not worship, because they had strength. Ibn al-Zubayr reportedly reached seven days.
rows.anchor: عن عبد الله بن الزبير وغيره من السلف، أنهم كانوا يواصلون الأيام المتعددة

rows.speaker: أبو العالية
rows.claim: Abū al-ʿĀliya says fasting is prescribed during the day, while at night a person may eat or choose not to eat.
rows.anchor: إنما فرض الله الصيام بالنهار فإذا جاء بالليل فمن شاء أكل ومن شاء لم يأكل

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās says anyone in iʿtikāf in a mosque, in Ramadan or otherwise, is forbidden from sexual relations with women by night or day until the retreat ends.
rows.anchor: فحرم الله عليه أن ينكح النساء ليلا ونهارا

rows.speaker: الضحاك
rows.claim: Al-Ḍaḥḥāk says a person formerly could leave the mosque during retreat and have intercourse; the verse now forbids approaching wives while one remains in iʿtikāf, inside or outside the mosque. Mujāhid, Qatāda, and others agree that this practice preceded the verse.
rows.anchor: كان الرجل إذا اعتكف فخرج من المسجد، جامع إن شاء، فقال الله تعالى: {ولا تباشروهن وأنتم عاكفون

rows.speaker: ابن مسعود، محمد بن كعب، مجاهد، عطاء، الحسن، قتادة، الضحاك، السدي، الربيع بن أنس، مقاتل
rows.claim: These early authorities agree that an iʿtikāf participant may not have intercourse with his wife during the retreat.
rows.anchor: روي عن ابن مسعود، ومحمد بن كعب، ومجاهد، وعطاء، والحسن، وقتادة، والضحاك والسدي، والربيع بن أنس، ومقاتل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: During iʿtikāf one may leave only as long as necessary for bodily needs; one may not kiss, embrace, occupy oneself with other matters, or visit the sick, though one may ask while passing.
rows.anchor: ليس له أن يقبل امرأته، ولا يضمها إليه، ولا يشتغل بشيء سوى اعتكافه، ولا يعود المريض

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Iʿtikāf has detailed rules, some agreed upon and others disputed, which Ibn Kathīr treated in the final part of his fasting book.
rows.anchor: وللاعتكاف أحكام مفصلة في بابه، منها ما هو مجمع عليه بين العلماء، ومنها ما هو مختلف فيه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Qur'an's placement of iʿtikāf after fasting points to retreat during fasting or in Ramadan's final part; the Prophet observed the last ten days yearly until death, and his wives continued afterward.
rows.anchor: وفي ذكره تعالى الاعتكاف بعد الصيام إرشاد وتنبيه على الاعتكاف في الصيام، أو في آخر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: During iʿtikāf, Ṣafiyya visited the Prophet at night; he escorted her home, explained her identity to two Anṣārī men, and said Satan moves through Adam's bloodstream and he feared an evil thought might enter their hearts.
rows.anchor: إن الشيطان يجري من ابن آدم مجرى الدم، وإني خشيت أن يقذف في قلوبكما شيئا

rows.speaker: الشافعي
rows.claim: Al-Shāfiʿī says the Prophet clarified himself to prevent suspicion in a place where suspicion might arise, protecting the two men from falling into error; they were too pious to think ill of him.
rows.anchor: أراد، عليه السلام، أن يعلم أمته التبري من التهمة في محلها، لئلا يقعا في محذور

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Direct marital contact forbidden during iʿtikāf includes intercourse and its preliminaries, such as kissing and embracing, but ordinary handling is permitted.
rows.anchor: ثم المراد بالمباشرة: إنما هو الجماع ودواعيه من تقبيل، ومعانقة ونحو ذلك

rows.speaker: عائشة
rows.claim: ʿĀʾisha reports that the Prophet let her comb his hair while she menstruated and entered the house only for a human need; she passed by a sick person to inquire about him.
rows.anchor: كان رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم يدني إلي رأسه فأرجله وأنا حائض

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “God's limits” are the fasting rules, prohibitions, permissions, endpoints, concessions, and obligations He defined; “do not approach them” means do not exceed them.
rows.anchor: هذا الذي بيناه، وفرضناه، وحددناه من الصيام، وأحكامه، وما أبحنا فيه وما حرمنا

rows.speaker: الضحاك، مقاتل
rows.claim: Al-Ḍaḥḥāk and Muqātil specifically interpret God's limits here as the prohibition on sexual contact during iʿtikāf; Ibn Zayd instead refers to four limits spanning night intercourse through completing the fast at night.
rows.anchor: وكان الضحاك ومقاتل يقولان في قوله تعالى: {تلك حدود الله} أي: المباشرة في الاعتكاف

rows.speaker: عبد الرحمن بن زيد بن أسلم
rows.claim: Ibn Zayd calls these four boundaries the sequence from night intimacy through completing the fast at night, as his elders taught him.
rows.anchor: وقال عبد الرحمن بن زيد بن أسلم: يعني هذه الحدود الأربعة، ويقرأ

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: As God details fasting here, He clarifies other rulings through Muhammad so people can find guidance and obey; Ibn Kathīr links this to the verse about bringing people from darkness to light.
rows.anchor: {كذلك يبين الله آياته للناس} أي: كما بين الصيام وأحكامه وشرائعه وتفاصيله

rows.speaker: علي بن أبي طالب، ابن عباس، الحسن، قتادة، السدي، سليمان بن بريدة
rows.claim: The well-known view identifies the passerby as ʿUzayr; ʿAlī is reported to say this, and Ibn ʿAbbās, al-Ḥasan, Qatāda, al-Suddī, and Sulaymān ibn Burayda also held it.
rows.anchor: عن علي بن أبي طالب أنه قال: هو عزير

rows.speaker: وهب بن منبه، عبد الله بن عبيد بن عمير
rows.claim: Wahb ibn Munabbih and ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿUbayd ibn ʿUmayr identify the passerby as Jeremiah son of Hilkiah.
rows.anchor: وقال وهب بن منبه وعبد الله بن عبيد بن عمير: هو أرميا بن حلقيا

rows.speaker: وهب بن منبه
rows.claim: In a report transmitted by Ibn Isḥāq from Wahb, the figure is called al-Khiḍr.
rows.anchor: عن وهب بن منبه أنه قال: وهو اسم الخضر عليه السلام

rows.speaker: رجل من أهل الشام
rows.claim: An unnamed Syrian informant identifies him as Ḥizqīl ibn Būrā.
rows.anchor: سمعت رجلا من أهل الشام يقول: إن الذي أماته الله مائة عام ثم بعثه اسمه: حزقيل بن بورا

rows.speaker: مجاهد بن جبر
rows.claim: Mujāhid identifies him simply as a man from the Children of Israel.
rows.anchor: وقال مجاهد بن جبر: هو رجل من بني إسرائيل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The village is famously identified as Jerusalem, after Nebuchadnezzar destroyed it and killed its inhabitants; khāwiyah means empty of people, from an Arabic expression for a vacant house.
rows.anchor: فالمشهور أنها بيت المقدس مر عليها بعد تخريب بختنصر لها وقتل أهلها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The village's roofs and walls had fallen into its open spaces; the man reflected on how it could return to life after such ruin.
rows.anchor: أي: ساقطة سقوفها وجدرانها على عرصاتها، فوقف متفكرا فيما آل أمرها إليه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The town was rebuilt seventy years after the man's death, its population grew, and the Israelites returned before God revived him after a century.
rows.anchor: وعمرت البلدة بعد مضي سبعين سنة من موته وتكامل ساكنوها وتراجعت بنو إسرائيل إليها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God first revived the man's eyes so he could watch how his body would be restored; revived near the end of the day, he thought only a day or part had passed because the sun remained.
rows.anchor: كان أول شيء أحيا الله فيه عينيه لينظر بهما إلى صنع الله فيه كيف يحيي بدنه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: His grapes, figs, and juice remained unchanged for a hundred years, while the donkey's revival was shown before his eyes as a sign for people and evidence of resurrection.
rows.anchor: كان معه فيما ذكر عنب وتين وعصير فوجده كما فقده لم يتغير منه شيء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The word nanshizuhā, with zāy, means raising the bones and fitting them together one over another.
rows.anchor: قرأ: {كيف ننشزها} بالزاي ثم قال: صحيح الإسناد ولم يخرجاه

rows.speaker: زيد بن ثابت
rows.claim: A report says the Prophet recited the word with zāy; al-Ḥākim called its chain sound, though the two Ṣaḥīḥ collections did not include it.
rows.anchor: أن رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم قرأ: {كيف ننشزها} بالزاي ثم قال: صحيح الإسناد ولم يخرجاه

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujāhid explains the variant recitation nanshuruhā, with rāʾ, as “revive them.”
rows.anchor: وقرئ: (ننشرها) أي: نحييها قاله مجاهد

rows.speaker: السدي وغيره
rows.claim: Al-Suddī and others say the donkey's scattered bones were gathered by a wind and reassembled; flesh, sinew, veins, and skin were restored, and an angel breathed into its nostrils until it brayed before ʿUzayr.
rows.anchor: وقال السدي وغيره: تفرقت عظام حماره حوله يمينا ويسارا

rows.speaker: قراءة أخرى
rows.claim: Another recitation makes the final verb a command, “Know,” addressed to the man rather than his statement, “I know.”
rows.anchor: وقرأ آخرون: "قال اعلم" على أنه أمر له بالعلم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The seed parable depicts God multiplying charity spent in His cause for His pleasure, from tenfold to seven hundredfold.
rows.anchor: لتضعيف الثواب لمن أنفق في سبيله وابتغاء مرضاته، وأن الحسنة تضاعف بعشر أمثالها

rows.speaker: سعيد بن جبير
rows.claim: Saʿīd ibn Jubayr interprets spending in God's cause as spending in obedience to Him.
rows.anchor: قال سعيد بن جبير: في طاعة الله

rows.speaker: مكحول
rows.claim: Makḥūl interprets it as military spending, including keeping horses ready, preparing weapons, and similar costs.
rows.anchor: وقال مكحول: يعني به: الإنفاق في الجهاد، من رباط الخيل وإعداد السلاح وغير ذلك

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās, through Shabīb ibn Bishr and ʿIkrima, applies it to jihad and pilgrimage, where a dirham can be multiplied seven hundredfold.
rows.anchor: وقال شبيب بن بشر، عن عكرمة، عن ابن عباس: الجهاد والحج، يضعف الدرهم فيهما إلى سبعمائة ضعف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The growing-seed image affects people more strongly than simply naming seven hundred because God nurtures good deeds like crops in fertile ground.
rows.anchor: وهذا المثل أبلغ في النفوس، من ذكر عدد السبعمائة، فإن هذا فيه إشارة إلى أن الأعمال الصالحة

rows.speaker: أبو عبيدة بن الجراح
rows.claim: The Prophet said surplus spending in God's cause earns seven hundredfold, while spending on oneself or family, visiting a sick person, or removing harm earns tenfold; fasting is a shield unless broken, and bodily affliction erases sins. A report is partly transmitted by al-Nasāʾī, including a mawqūf version.
rows.anchor: من أنفق نفقة فاضلة في سبيل الله فبسبعمائة، ومن أنفق على نفسه وأهله، أو عاد مريضا

rows.speaker: عبد الله بن مسعود
rows.claim: The Prophet said that whoever gives a branded she-camel in God's cause will receive seven hundred branded camels at the Resurrection.
rows.anchor: عن ابن مسعود: أن رجلا تصدق بناقة مخطومة في سبيل الله، فقال رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم

rows.speaker: عبد الله بن مسعود
rows.claim: Muslim's wording has a man bring a branded camel as a gift for God's cause, and the Prophet promises seven hundred camels in return.
rows.anchor: جاء رجل بناقة مخطومة، فقال: يا رسول الله، هذه في سبيل الله

rows.speaker: عبد الله بن مسعود
rows.claim: The Prophet says good deeds are multiplied tenfold to seven hundred except fasting, which belongs to God and He rewards; the fasting person has two joys and a scent more pleasing than musk.
rows.anchor: إن الله عز وجل، جعل حسنة ابن آدم بعشر أمثالها، إلى سبعمائة ضعف، إلا الصوم، والصوم لي وأنا أجزي به

rows.speaker: أبو هريرة
rows.claim: The Prophet says deeds are multiplied tenfold up to seven hundred or more, except fasting, which is for God; the fasting person leaves food and desire for Him, enjoys breaking the fast and meeting Him, and has a scent dearer to God than musk. Fasting is a shield.
rows.anchor: كل عمل ابن آدم يضاعف، الحسنة بعشر أمثالها إلى سبعمائة ضعف

rows.speaker: خريم بن فاتك
rows.claim: The Prophet said spending in God's cause is multiplied seven hundredfold.
rows.anchor: من أنفق نفقة في سبيل الله تضاعف بسبعمائة

rows.speaker: معاذ بن جبل
rows.claim: A report says prayer, fasting, and remembrance receive a seven-hundredfold multiplier in relation to spending in God's cause.
rows.anchor: إن الصلاة والصيام والذكر يضاعف على النفقة في سبيل الله سبعمائة ضعف

rows.speaker: عمران بن حصين
rows.claim: A strange report says a person who funds an expedition while staying home receives seven hundred per dirham, while one who goes out and spends receives seven hundred thousand per dirham; the Prophet then recited this verse.
rows.anchor: من أرسل بنفقة في سبيل الله، وأقام في بيته

rows.speaker: أبو هريرة
rows.claim: A report previously cited at 2:245 says a good deed may be multiplied to two million good deeds.
rows.anchor: وقد تقدم حديث أبي عثمان النهدي، عن أبي هريرة في تضعيف الحسنة إلى ألفي ألف حسنة

rows.speaker: ابن عمر
rows.claim: When this verse was revealed, the Prophet asked God to increase his community's reward; 2:245 followed, then after another request 39:10 came down. Ibn Ḥibbān also transmits the report in his Ṣaḥīḥ.
rows.anchor: لما نزلت هذه الآية: {مثل الذين ينفقون أموالهم في سبيل الله} قال النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم: "رب زد أمتي"

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God's multiplication varies according to the spender's sincerity.
rows.anchor: أي: بحسب إخلاصه في عمله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God is vast in abundant bounty and knows who deserves it and who does not.
rows.anchor: فضله واسع كثير أكثر من خلقه، عليم بمن يستحق ومن لا يستحق

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God praises those who give in His cause and then neither boast to recipients nor remind them of their gift in word or deed.
rows.anchor: فلا يمنون على أحد، ولا يمنون به لا بقول ولا فعل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: They do not mistreat beneficiaries in a way that cancels their earlier kindness; their reward is with God, they need not fear future terrors, and they will not grieve over lost family or worldly pleasures.
rows.anchor: لا يفعلون مع من أحسنوا إليه مكروها يحبطون به ما سلف من الإحسان

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A kind word and prayer for a Muslim, together with forgiving verbal or physical wrong, are better than charity followed by harm.
rows.anchor: من كلمة طيبة ودعاء لمسلم

rows.speaker: رسول الله
rows.claim: A report reaching ʿAmr ibn Dīnār says no charity is more beloved to God than a good word, citing this verse.
rows.anchor: بلغنا أن رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم قال: "ما من صدقة أحب إلى الله من قول معروف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God has no need of His creatures; He is forbearing, forgiving, and overlooking.
rows.anchor: عن خلقه. {حليم} أي: يحلم ويغفر ويصفح ويتجاوز عنهم

rows.speaker: أبو ذر
rows.claim: The Prophet warned of painful punishment for three people: one who flaunts what he gave, one who lets his garment trail, and a merchant who uses false oaths.
rows.anchor: عن أبي ذر قال: قال رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم: "ثلاثة لا يكلمهم الله يوم القيامة

rows.speaker: أبو الدرداء
rows.claim: A report says that a person disobedient to parents, one who flaunts charity, a habitual wine drinker, and a denier of divine decree do not enter Paradise; other transmitters report a similar version.
rows.anchor: عن أبي الدرداء، عن النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم قال: "لا يدخل الجنة عاق، ولا منان، ولا مدمن خمر

rows.speaker: ابن عمر
rows.claim: Another prophetic report lists the disobedient child, habitual wine drinker, and person who flaunts gifts among three whom God will not look upon at the Resurrection.
rows.anchor: ثلاثة لا ينظر الله إليهم يوم القيامة: العاق لوالديه، ومدمن الخمر، والمنان بما أعطى

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: A report through Mujāhid says habitual wine drinkers, those disobedient to parents, and those who flaunt gifts do not enter Paradise; other transmissions attribute related reports to Mujāhid from Abū Saʿīd and Abū Hurayra.
rows.anchor: قال: "لا يدخل الجنة مدمن خمر، ولا عاق لوالديه، ولا منان"

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse declares that flaunting a gift or harming its recipient nullifies charity, so its reward cannot outweigh the sin of those acts.
rows.anchor: فأخبر أن الصدقة تبطل بما يتبعها من المن والأذى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A show-off gives to win public praise or a reputation for generosity while neglecting God's approval and reward; his deeds vanish like rain washing soil off smooth rock, even if people see apparent good works.
rows.anchor: فأظهر لهم أنه يريد وجه الله وإنما قصده مدح الناس له أو شهرته بالصفات الجميلة

rows.speaker: الضحاك
rows.claim: Al-Ḍaḥḥāk explains the hypocritical spender's likeness as also covering someone who follows a gift with boasting or harm.
rows.anchor: قال الضحاك: والذي يتبع نفقته منا أو أذى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Believers who give seeking God's pleasure do so with conviction that He will reward them fully; this resembles the authenticated report about fasting Ramadan in faith and seeking reward.
rows.anchor: وهم متحققون مثبتون أن الله سيجزيهم على ذلك أوفر الجزاء

rows.speaker: الشعبي، قتادة، أبو صالح، ابن زيد
rows.claim: Al-Shaʿbī interprets the phrase as affirmation and certainty; Qatāda, Abū Ṣāliḥ, and Ibn Zayd agree, and Ibn Jarīr selects this view.
rows.anchor: قال الشعبي: {وتثبيتا من أنفسهم} أي: تصديقا ويقينا

rows.speaker: مجاهد، الحسن
rows.claim: Mujāhid and al-Ḥasan instead say that donors carefully establish where to place their charity.
rows.anchor: وقال مجاهد والحسن: أي: يتثبتون أين يضعون

rows.speaker: الجمهور، ابن عباس، الضحاك
rows.claim: Most commentators define a rabwa as level ground at an elevated place; Ibn ʿAbbās and al-Ḍaḥḥāk add that streams run there.
rows.anchor: وهو عند الجمهور: المكان المرتفع المستوي من الأرض. وزاد ابن عباس والضحاك: وتجري فيه الأنهار

rows.speaker: ابن جرير
rows.claim: Ibn Jarīr notes three dialectal and recitational forms of rabwa: with ḍamma, common in Medina, the Ḥijāz, and Iraq; fatḥa, used by some Syrians and Kūfans and attributed to Tamīm; and kasra, reported as Ibn ʿAbbās's reading.
rows.anchor: قال ابن جرير: وفي الربوة ثلاث لغات هن ثلاث قراءات: بضم الراء، وبها قرأ عامة أهل المدينة والحجاز والعراق

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Wābil is heavy rain, ukul is fruit, and ḍiʿfayn means twice the yield compared with other gardens.
rows.anchor: وهو المطر الشديد، كما تقدم

rows.speaker: الضحاك
rows.claim: Al-Ḍaḥḥāk says ṭall is drizzle, a gentle rain; the high garden is sustained by either heavy rain or drizzle, just as a believer's work is never wasted but accepted and multiplied according to the person's deeds.
rows.anchor: قال الضحاك: هو الرذاذ، وهو اللين من المطر.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God sees everything His servants do, and none of their deeds is hidden from Him.
rows.anchor: لا يخفى عليه من أعمال عباده شيء
